title: Predictive Leash scaler: contract-aware, KV-warmup and smoothing safety policy
creator: Miguel Torres
description: Design and implement a new autoscaling policy (Predictive Leash) for Redwood Dedicated fleets that enforces throughput guarantees while minimizing oscillation and respecting KV-cache warmup affinity. The policy blends demand forecasting, contract-backed headroom, and a smoothing/hysteresis layer to provide tenant-level throughput contracts with fleet-level safety limits.
motivation: Current autoscalers either react too aggressively (causing costly churn) or too conservatively (causing SLA violations). We need a policy that can: 1) guarantee committed throughput for paying tenants, 2) avoid painful scale flip-flops during bursty traffic, 3) prefer warm lanes (KV cache affinity) when deciding to open capacity, and 4) cap costs via explicit safety fences and rollback windows.
design_notes: Policy components: forecast module (simple ETS or short LSTM-lite), contract headroom translator, smoothing/hysteresis controller, KV-warmup penalty function, safety fences and rollback windows.

Target metrics: tenant 95th/99th token throughput per second, per-tenant p50/p95 latency, and committed throughput credit balance. Policy computes desired 'capacity units' (GPU slots) to meet target percentile given recent token distribution and forecasted load.

Smoothing algorithm: two-stage filter — short-term EWMA for responsiveness, long-term ramp limiter (max X% change per Y minutes) to prevent step-changes. Add derivative damping to avoid reacting to transient spikes.

KV-warmup affinity: when deciding between adding new slot versus reassigning warm lanes, compute warmup cost (estimated cold KV miss penalty in p90 latency & token cost) and favor assignments that preserve hot prefix affinity if warmup cost > threshold.

Safety fences: global fleet cap (absolute limit, set per SKU), per-tenant cap derived from contract, and a shared surge budget. Each scale-up is tagged with a short TTL and rollback window; if latencies don't improve within window, automatically revert.
Fallbacks: if forecast fails or telemetry gaps exist, fallback to conservative percentile-based estimator (e.g., use 99.9th observed rate over trailing window).
Observability: expose per-decision telemetry (forecast input, chosen capacity delta, which safety fence triggered, warmup penalty applied) to Console and runtime tracing.
Config surface: allow operators to tune forecast horizon, smoothing alpha values, max ramp percent, warmup penalty thresholds, rollback windows, and surge budget allocations.
Backward compatibility: policy will implement the existing autoscaler DSL interface and be plumbed behind a feature flag on Dedicated clusters for gradual rollout.
Security: no customer data is required in forecasting; use aggregated token counts and anonymized route identifiers.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (spike, 2w): build lightweight forecast prototype using ETS and integrate with simulator to compare against historical traces. Deliverables: forecast lib, simulator harness extension.
Phase 2 (policy core, 3w): implement capacity translator, smoothing controller, warmup penalty integration, and safety-fence checks. Unit tests for each module.
Phase 3 (integration, 2w): wire policy into autoscaler control plane, add decision telemetry, and implement rollback executor.
Phase 4 (canary rollout, 2w): enable behind feature flag on test region; monitor efficacy vs baseline on latency and cost metrics, iterate.
Phase 5 (wide rollout, 1w): gated roll to remaining Dedicated fleets once acceptance criteria met.
acceptance_criteria: Policy computes capacity deltas deterministically given replayed traces in the simulator and matches expected bounds from design doc.
Canary clusters show >=95% reduction in oscillation events (flip-flop scale-ups/downs) compared to baseline autoscaler on workload X and comparable or improved p95 latency for committed tenants.
Warmup-aware decisions demonstrate measurable reduction in cold-KV miss events (>=30% reduction) and reduce end-to-end p95 latency during bursts for warm tenants.
Rollback triggers function: when rollback condition met in canary, policy reverts and controller records a rollforward/rollback event in tracing UI.
All new telemetry surfaces in Console (per-decision logs, safety-fence reasons, warmup_penalty) with retention suitable for debugging.
No customer-visible regressions in unrelated routes; existing e2e smoke tests pass.
Security review completed and signed off if required.
Documentation: operator runbook and config reference published in Confluence/Console help.
rollout_plan: 1) Internal dry-run: run policy in 'simulate' mode for 1 week against production traces — no control plane changes.
2) Canary: enable on 2 small Dedicated fleets (non-critical), monitor for 72h, then 7d extended window.
3) Gradual expansion: incrementally increase to 25% of fleets, then 60%, then full (gated on SLA metrics).
4) Rollback plan: feature flag off instantly reverts decision engine. For persistent regressions, automatic rollback executor will decommission scale changes created in last 30m.
5) Communication: notify SRE and Customer Success teams before canary; publish known caveats and monitoring dashboards.
test_plan: Simulator tests: replay representative tenant traces (PLG traffic, enterprise commit patterns, bursty mobile traffic) and assert capacity changes within spec.
Integration tests: end-to-end on test clusters validating KV-warmup metrics, decision telemetry, and rollback paths.
Chaos tests: inject delayed telemetry and simulate partial failures to ensure safe fallback estimator is used.
Load tests: synthetic traffic to validate max ramp percent and surge budget behaviour under sustained increases.
Regression tests: run standard autoscaler regression suite and ensure no performance degradations.
dependencies: ENG-612345 (predictive warmup autoscaler) - reference traces and simulator harness
ENG-42177 (observability: per-decision tracing) - decision telemetry endpoint
Infra: quota update for surge budget feature flag rollout
notes: Trade-offs considered: heavy ML forecasting increases complexity and ops cost; we opt for lightweight ETS + feature flags to allow upgrading to an LSTM if accuracy proves insufficient.
Potential follow-ups: per-tenant historical affinity maps, dynamic surge budget rebalancer, and integration with cost-predictor for committed contract billing alignment.
Open question: precise mapping from percentile throughput to capacity units — propose initial table then tune via canary.
Stakeholder signoffs required: SRE, PM (capacity guarantees), Security if forecast inputs change.
